paras: The Brookside riot was an armed clash on the night of July 30, 1895, at a Sloss Iron and Steel Company mining camp west of Birmingham, Alabama, in which white miners fought and pursued Black miners after Deputy Sheriff A. T. Wood was shot dead making an arrest. Wire reports said three or four Black men were killed and that white miners had captives beneath a noose when Sheriff Morrow forced their surrender, though the local Birmingham Age-Herald discredited the reports of bodies. Papers nationwide carried it as a "race riot," and the rescue drew editorial comment.

According to the Associated Press, Mine Boss Culverhouse had discharged a Black miner, Jim Biggers or Biggars in most printings and Jim Smith in one, and a trespass warrant followed when he refused to leave company premises. The Age-Herald instead traced the fight to a quarrel between a brother of Charlie Jenkins and Boss Driver Harris.

Wood, a former sheriff of Talladega County, went to make the arrest with Joel Baxter, a citizen sworn in as special deputy, and was shot dead. The wire said the wanted man fired a Winchester, while the Age-Herald reported that officers and eyewitnesses named another man, Gardiner, as Wood's killer and that George Hill was also seen shooting.

White miners then organized and fought a Black party, described as entrenched in a ditch, for one to two hours. The fullest dispatch described two battles with two Black men shot dead in each, after which the Black party fled into the woods with white miners in pursuit; more than a dozen whites were wounded.

Sheriff Morrow arrived from Birmingham with about 25 men around midnight and found several Black captives "bound hand and foot" beneath a noose hung from a tree limb. The white miners' leader refused two demands, and gave up the prisoners only when the sheriff threatened to fire on both parties and his men raised their arms. The Raleigh News and Observer named two of the men with ropes about their necks as Will Albert and Charles Jenkins.

The Age-Herald reported eight men jailed in Birmingham after three or four were released, while the wire gave ten or eleven and said officers sought twelve more. James Bridges, called a leader of the Black party, was captured the next morning; a Nashville dispatch said lynching "was talked of, but was not attempted." One dispatch said Bob Simms, or Bob Williams in another printing, was found dying in a cabin, but no Black dead were named.

The preliminary trial of "Jenkins and others" was postponed twice, and on August 22 Charles Green was discharged and Wade Blockton held without bail. On September 10 George Hill was indicted for the first-degree murder of Arthur T. Woods "at the time of the Brookside riots." No report of an inquest, a verdict, or charges against the white miners appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press story ran on August 1 from Maine to Texas under headlines such as "A BLOODY RACE RIOT" and "NEGROES SAVED FROM A MOB," calling the Black men "rioters" who poured "a murderous fire" on officers.

Editorial responses diverged. The Kansas City Journal predicted "a general lynching of the negroes" and wrote that the colored race "is always goaded into aggression and then punished for defending their rights." The Chicago Inter Ocean, reprinted in The Mirror, praised the sheriff's stand against the mob while accepting that the Black prisoners were "the aggressive parties," and the Wheeling Register blamed foreign immigrants for the friction.

In Birmingham the Age-Herald headed its report "ALL IS QUIET AT BROOKSIDE" and later asked whether special correspondents had distorted the "alleged 'race riot'" in Jefferson County. Congressman Cobb of Alabama said Southern affairs "are never fairly represented in the North" and offered a different version of the "race war." No coverage in the Black press was found.

The wire said both deputies died, but the Age-Herald, whose reporter saw Baxter the next morning, described a flesh wound in the leg, and the later charges concerned Wood alone. Reports of Black deaths ranged from three to "half a dozen," while the Age-Herald found no one who knew of the bodies.

reader.title: Brookside riot (1895)
bases: Wire reports describe a running gun battle between armed white miners and a group of Black miners at the Brookside camp after a deputy was shot, with Black men reported shot dead in the pursuit and captives bound under a noose before the sheriff took them (A3, A4, A5); the local paper confirms the fight and the deputy's death (A2).

The local Birmingham Age-Herald (A2) and the Associated Press wire (A3, A4, A17) independently report the shooting of Deputy Wood, the fight and the arrests, though the local paper disputes the reported Black deaths and Baxter's death.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: The discharged miner fired a Winchester on the two deputies, killing both; his friends entrenched in a ditch fought white miners for up to two hours; three or four Black men were killed, and captives were about to be hanged when Sheriff Morrow forced their surrender.

accounts.label: Birmingham Age-Herald (local)
accounts.gist: The fight grew from a quarrel between a Jenkins brother and Boss Driver Harris; officers name Gardiner and Hill as shooters; Baxter has a leg flesh wound; the report of dead bodies was discredited.

accounts.label: Congressman Cobb
accounts.gist: A white man tried to thrash a hired Black boy, the boy's brothers and other Black men resisted, an officer sent to drive them off was shot dead, and one Black man was wounded in the leg; the place is not named.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'A BLOODY RACE RIOT', 'NEGROES SAVED FROM A MOB' and 'BROUGHT IN TEN RIOTERS' presented the Black men as 'rioters' who poured 'a murderous fire' on officers.
The Kansas City Journal predicted 'a general lynching of the negroes' and wrote that the colored race is 'goaded into aggression and then punished'.
The Chicago Inter Ocean, reprinted in The Mirror, praised the sheriff for saving negroes from 'the vengeance of the mob' while calling them 'the aggressive parties'.

The Birmingham Age-Herald's editorial called it an 'alleged "race riot"' and blamed sensational special correspondents; Congressman Cobb said Southern affairs are never fairly represented in the North.
The Wheeling Register blamed 'the new element of foreign immigration' for the friction behind the Alabama race riots.

record_check.dossier: Mixes roles: Wood (A. T., not A. I.) and Baxter were the deputies; Jim Smith and Jim Biggers are one wanted man in two wire versions; Bob Simms and Bob Williams are one dying man; Bridges and Jenkins were accused prisoners. Victims of white violence are the unnamed Black dead, Simms/Williams, and the captives Will Albert and Charles Jenkins.
The hanging of the captives was attempted and stopped by the sheriff; the reported Black deaths came in the shooting and pursuit, not at the noose.
in_pursuit: the captives were seized by white miners in the woods and taken from them by the sheriff, not taken from officers; a later attempt at the camp to take them from the sheriff failed.
